patient.name: Renee Castillo
patient.chiefComplaint: Progressive shortness of breath not relieved by rescue inhaler

history.hpi: Patient with known asthma since childhood reports worsening shortness of breath over the past hour after a URI this week. Used her albuterol MDI four times in the last 45 minutes with minimal relief before calling 911. No fever, no chest pain, no known trigger exposure today.
history.lastOralIntake: Dinner approximately 3 hours prior to symptom onset
history.events: Developed progressive dyspnea after a several-day upper respiratory infection; overused home rescue inhaler without relief and called 911

scene.location: Second-floor apartment, patient seated on living room couch
scene.bystanders: Roommate present, states patient has been "wheezing badly" for the last hour and has used her inhaler repeatedly
visualCues: Patient sitting upright, leaning forward, hands on knees (tripod)
Visible accessory muscle use with intercostal retractions
Empty albuterol MDI canister on the coffee table
Audible expiratory wheeze from across the room

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find a 34-year-old female in moderate-to-severe respiratory distress, tripod positioning, with audible wheezing and accessory muscle use. She reports overusing her rescue inhaler without relief.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Labored, prolonged expiratory phase, intercostal and subcostal retractions, audible wheezing bilaterally
otherFindings: Diffuse expiratory wheezing on auscultation, diminished air entry at bases
clinicalPresentation.patientSpeech: "Can't... catch my breath... inhaler's not working."

transitions.condition: Crew applies supplemental oxygen and administers nebulized albuterol/ipratropium for signs of bronchospasm with respiratory distress.

phases.name: Oxygen and nebulized bronchodilators given
phases.description: Crew administers supplemental oxygen and nebulized albuterol/ipratropium. Despite treatment, the patient shows minimal improvement and remains in significant distress.
phases.triggerCondition: After recognizing signs of bronchospasm with respiratory distress, the crew applies oxygen and begins nebulized albuterol and ipratropium per protocol, but the patient does not respond adequately.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent, still speaking in short phrases
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Persistent labored breathing, continued retractions, wheezing largely unchanged

expectedActions.shortAction: Administer supplemental O2 titrated to target SpO2 94-98%
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Give supplemental oxygen for dyspnea to a target of 94–98% saturation. Escalate from a nasal cannula as needed to reach this goal
expectedActions.rationale: Corrects hypoxemia while other therapies take effect.

expectedActions.shortAction: Albuterol 5 mg nebulized for bronchospasm with respiratory distress
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: albuterol 5 mg nebulized (or 6 puffs metered dose inhaler) should be administered to all patients in respiratory distress with signs of bronchospasm (e.g., known asthmatics, quiet wheezers). Repeat at this dose with unlimited frequency for ongoing respiratory distress
expectedActions.rationale: First-line bronchodilator for asthma exacerbation with distress.

expectedActions.shortAction: Ipratropium 0.5 mg nebulized in conjunction with albuterol
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Ipratropium 0.5 mg nebulized should be given up to 3 doses in conjunction with albuterol
expectedActions.rationale: Adjunct bronchodilator that may decrease need for hospital admission when combined with albuterol.

expectedActions.shortAction: Apply continuous pulse oximetry and waveform capnography
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Patients with significant respiratory distress should have continuous pulse oximetry and waveform capnography monitoring for both assessment and for guiding therapy
expectedActions.rationale: A rising or normalizing EtCO2 despite tachypnea signals impending respiratory failure.

transitions.condition: Given persistent severe distress despite nebulized bronchodilators, the crew escalates to non-invasive ventilation (CPAP) with nebulized medication administered in line.
Crew continues nebulized treatments alone without escalating to non-invasive ventilation despite persistent severe distress, allowing progression toward respiratory failure.

phases.name: CPAP with in-line duoneb started
phases.description: Crew escalates to CPAP with nebulized albuterol/ipratropium administered in line through a T-connector. The patient begins to show improved air movement and decreased work of breathing.
phases.triggerCondition: Persistent severe respiratory distress despite nebulized bronchodilators meets criteria for non-invasive ventilation; CPAP is applied with continued nebulized medication delivered in line.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Improved air entry, decreased accessory muscle use, mask seal maintained
otherFindings: CPAP mask in place with continuous seal

expectedActions.shortAction: Initiate CPAP with nebulizer administered in-line via T-connector
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) should be administered for severe respiratory distress via BVM, continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) or bi-level positive airway pressure (BiPAP). If indicated, bronchodilators should be administered in line with NIV. Nebulized medications may be administered through a CPAP or BiPAP mask. A specialized T-connector with a spring valve assembly is required to allow maintenance of positive airway pressure
expectedActions.rationale: Escalates support for persistent severe bronchospasm not responding to nebulizers alone.

expectedActions.shortAction: Maintain continuous CPAP mask seal; do not discontinue en route
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Once initiated and patient is tolerating mask, DO NOT discontinue CPAP/BiPAP until patient is on the emergency department stretcher and hospital CPAP/BiPAP is immediately available for patient to be switched over, or physician is at bedside and requesting CPAP/BiPAP be discontinued. Breaking the mask seal causes a significant decrease in airway pressures and may lead to abrupt decompensation due to atelectasis and alveolar collapse
expectedActions.rationale: Breaking the seal risks abrupt decompensation from lost airway pressure.

transitions.if: Improved on CPAP, prepared for transport
transitions.condition: Patient's work of breathing and oxygenation improve on CPAP with in-line bronchodilator; crew packages for transport while maintaining the mask seal.

phases.name: Improved on CPAP, prepared for transport
phases.description: Patient remains on CPAP with in-line nebulized bronchodilator during transport, with improved oxygenation and decreased work of breathing.
phases.triggerCondition: After CPAP and in-line bronchodilator therapy improve the patient's respiratory status, the crew continues therapy and transports with ongoing reassessment.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Mild residual distress, much improved air entry
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Radial pulses present bilaterally, rate improving
otherFindings: Improved wheeze, better air movement bilaterally

expectedActions.shortAction: Reassess respiratory status, SpO2, and EtCO2 serially en route
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Ongoing assessment is critical when an airway device is in place. Acute worsening of respiratory status or evidence of hypoxemia can be secondary to displacement or obstruction of the airway device
expectedActions.rationale: Ensures continued response to therapy and early detection of deterioration.

phases.name: CPAP escalation delayed
phases.description: Crew continues nebulized bronchodilators alone without escalating to non-invasive ventilation. The patient tires, air movement worsens, and EtCO2 begins normalizing despite ongoing tachypnea — an ominous sign of impending respiratory failure.
phases.triggerCondition: Persistent severe distress with minimal response to nebulized therapy is not escalated to CPAP; the patient progressively fatigues toward respiratory failure.

clinicalPresentation.breathing: Shallow, rapid, diminishing air entry bilaterally, minimal audible wheeze (ominous quiet chest)
otherFindings: EtCO2 normalizing/rising despite continued tachypnea — impending respiratory failure

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize impending respiratory failure from normalizing EtCO2 despite tachypnea
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Normal EtCO2 (35–45 mmHg) with tachypnea and respiratory distress is an indicator of impending respiratory failure
expectedActions.rationale: A quiet chest and normalizing EtCO2 in a tachypneic asthmatic signals exhaustion, not improvement.

expectedActions.shortAction: Emergently escalate to CPAP or assisted BVM ventilation with in-line bronchodilator
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Non-invasive ventilation (NIV) should be considered early for severe respiratory distress or impending respiratory failure. Use bag-valve-mask (BVM) ventilation in the setting of respiratory failure or arrest
expectedActions.rationale: Delayed escalation risks progression to full respiratory arrest.
